title: My day
goal: Tell the time and describe your daily routine — while facing verbs that split in two and send half of themselves to the end of the sentence.
bekal: use separable verbs (*Ich stehe um sechs auf*)
describe the order of your daily activities

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ein ganz normaler Tag
dialogs.intro: Lena asks about Budi's daily schedule. Watch the little word that turns up at the end of the sentence — *auf*, *an*, *ein* — and see where it comes from.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: What time do you get up in the morning?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich stehe um halb sieben auf. Manchmal um sieben.
lines.id: I get up at six-thirty. Sometimes at seven.
lines.literal: I stand at half seven up. sometimes at seven.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Und wann fängt der Kurs an?
lines.id: And when does the course start?
lines.literal: and when catches the course on?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Der Kurs fängt um neun Uhr an und hört um zwölf auf.
lines.id: The course starts at nine and finishes at twelve.
lines.literal: the course catches at nine o'clock on and hears at twelve up.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.id: What do you do in the afternoon?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ich lerne bis vier, dann kaufe ich ein.
lines.id: I study until four, then I go shopping.
lines.literal: I learn until four, then buy I in.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja, ich koche um Viertel nach sechs. Um acht rufe ich meine Eltern an.
lines.id: Yes, I cook at a quarter past six. At eight I call my parents.
lines.literal: yes, I cook at quarter after six. at eight call I my parents on.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: In Indonesien ist es dann schon Mitternacht, oder?
lines.id: It's already midnight in Indonesia by then, isn't it?
lines.literal: in Indonesia is it then already midnight, or?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Fast. Es ist ein Uhr nachts. Meine Mutter schläft nie früh.
lines.id: Almost. It's one in the morning. My mother never goes to bed early.
lines.literal: almost. it is one o'clock at-night. my mother sleeps never early.

lines.speaker: Lena:
lines.text: Und wann gehst du ins Bett?
lines.id: And when do you go to bed?
lines.literal: and when go you into-the bed?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Um Viertel vor elf. Aber heute sehe ich noch einen Film.
lines.id: At a quarter to eleven. But today I'm still watching a movie.
lines.literal: at quarter before eleven. but today see I still a film.

notes: **Verbs that split in two.** *aufstehen* (get up) becomes *ich stehe … **auf***; *anfangen* (start) becomes *der Kurs fängt … **an***; *einkaufen* (shop) becomes *ich kaufe … **ein***. The prefix flies to the end of the sentence, and everything else stands in between. English does something similar with phrasal verbs (*I get up*, *I call my parents up*) — German just always sends the little word to the very end. The grammar box below shows how it works.
***um* for an exact time.** *um sieben*, *um halb acht*, *um Viertel nach sechs*. For a range, use *von … bis*: *von neun bis zwölf*. For an end point alone, *bis* is enough: *Ich lerne bis vier*.

**⚠️ *halb sieben* = 6:30, not 7:30.** German counts the half hour **toward** the next hour: "half (on the way to) seven". English speakers trip badly here, because *half past six* points the other way. Every time you see *halb*, subtract thirty minutes from the number you hear.

***Uhr* is required with official whole hours**, and can be dropped in casual speech: *um neun Uhr* or *um neun*. But never use *Stunde* for clock time — *Stunde* is a length of time ("two hours"), *Uhr* is a point in time ("two o'clock").

**Parts of the day take *am*, except night.** *am Morgen*, *am Vormittag*, *am Nachmittag*, *am Abend* — but ***in der Nacht***, because *Nacht* is feminine. There are also adverb forms without a preposition, which sound more casual: *morgens*, *abends*, *nachts*.

**Lines 6 and 8: *dann kaufe ich ein* and *Um acht rufe ich … an*.** A sentence starting with a time expression still puts its verb in second place — and the separable prefix still goes to the end. Two rules working at once, and Germans use both without thinking.

grammars.title: Telling time: two ways, one clock
body: German has two systems living side by side. The **official** one uses the numbers 0-24 and is used on train timetables, broadcasts and formal appointments. The **everyday** one uses 1-12 with *nach*, *vor* and *halb*.
after: ⚠️ The **8:30 a.m.** row is where every English speaker slips: *halb neun* counts **toward** the next hour. Read it as "half to nine", never "half past nine".
Two questions to keep apart: ***Wie spät ist es?*** ("what time is it?") and ***Wann…?*** ("when?"). The answer to the first starts with *Es ist…*; the answer to the second starts with *Um…*

grammars.title: Separable verbs (trennbare Verben)
body: Some German verbs are made of **prefix + verb**: *auf + stehen*, *an + fangen*, *ein + kaufen*. In the dictionary they're written as one word, but as soon as they're used in a sentence, the prefix breaks off and flies to the end.

Everything else — object, time, place — stands between the two parts. This structure is called the **Satzklammer**, the "sentence bracket", because the verb really does bracket the content of the sentence.
after: The prefixes that most often split off: **auf-, an-, ein-, aus-, mit-, ab-, zu-, vor-, nach-, zurück-, fern-, weg-**. They're all short words that also stand alone as prepositions or adverbs, and they're all **stressed** when spoken: *AUFstehen*, *ANrufen*.

On the other hand, the prefixes **be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, emp-, zer-** never split off and are never stressed: *beSUchen* (to visit) → *Ich besuche meine Oma*, in one piece. This difference in stress is how a German ear recognizes the type, long before the sentence is over.

⚠️ If there's a helper verb like *möchten* or *können*, the separable verb **joins back together** and moves to the end: *Ich möchte um sechs **aufstehen***. The rules don't clash — only one thing is allowed at the end of the sentence.

rows: Ich gehe um acht zur Arbeit.
Ich gehe um elf ins Bett.

blocks.text: *Frühstücken* is one of the few verbs born from a noun (*das Frühstück*, breakfast). It's completely regular, and it does **not** split, even though it looks as if it starts with a *früh-* prefix.

sections.title: Telling the story of one day

blocks.text: Write your own daily routine using the pattern below. What matters isn't the length, but that every sentence contains a time — that's where separable verbs show up most.

items: *Ich stehe um … auf.* — I get up at …
*Dann frühstücke ich und dusche.* — Then I have breakfast and shower.
*Um … fängt meine Arbeit an.* — At … my work starts.
*Ich arbeite von … bis …* — I work from … to …
*Am Abend kaufe ich ein und koche.* — In the evening I go shopping and cook.
*Um … gehe ich ins Bett.* — At … I go to bed.

blocks.title: Test yourself: where does the prefix go?
items: *Ich … meine Mutter … (anrufen, um acht)* → **Ich rufe um acht meine Mutter an.**
*Wir … um zwölf … (aufhören)* → **Wir hören um zwölf auf.**
*… du heute Abend …? (mitkommen)* → **Kommst du heute Abend mit?**
